title: Where is the post office?
goal: Ask for and give directions, use prepositions of place, and form commands.
bekal: asking the way and — the harder part — understanding the answer
prepositions of place: *in, op, naast, tegenover, tussen*
wave: Go back to **unit 9**: tell your day from getting up to going to bed in ten sentences, each one opening with a time expression so the verb flips.

dialogs.title: Dialog — De weg vragen
dialogs.intro: Budi is lost in the city center. A canal, once again, looks exactly like the previous one.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Pardon, mag ik u iets vragen?
lines.id: Excuse me, may I ask you something?
lines.literal: pardon, may I you something ask?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Weet u waar het postkantoor is?
lines.id: Do you know where the post office is?
lines.literal: know you where the post-office is?

lines.speaker: Vrouw:
lines.text: Loop hier rechtdoor tot aan de brug.
lines.id: Go straight on here as far as the bridge.
lines.literal: walk here straight-ahead till at the bridge.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tot aan de brug. En dan?
lines.id: As far as the bridge. And then?
lines.literal: till at the bridge. and then?

lines.speaker: Vrouw:
lines.text: Ga daar linksaf, langs de gracht.
lines.id: Turn left there, along the canal.
lines.literal: go there left-off, along the canal.

lines.speaker: Vrouw:
lines.text: Nee hoor, vijf minuten lopen. Het zit naast de apotheek.
lines.id: Oh no, five minutes on foot. It's next to the pharmacy.
lines.literal: no really, five minutes walk. it sits next-to the pharmacy.

lines.speaker: Vrouw:
lines.text: Precies. Tussen de apotheek en de bakker.
lines.id: Exactly. Between the pharmacy and the bakery.
lines.literal: precisely. between the pharmacy and the baker.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thank you! Have a nice day.

notes: **Weet u waar het postkantoor is?** — notice the verb at the end (*is*), because the clause hangs on *waar*. This is called a subordinate clause; unit 20 takes it apart. For now, memorize the pattern: *Weet u waar … is?*
**Loop rechtdoor** — commands are formed from the verb stem, with no subject. Details in the grammar box.
**Linksaf / rechtsaf** — turn left / right. Note the attached *-af*; without it, *links* and *rechts* just mean "on the left" and "on the right".

**De gracht** is a city canal lined with houses — unlike *het kanaal* (a big canal between cities) and *de sloot* (a ditch between fields). Dutch has a far more detailed water vocabulary than most languages, and that is no accident: a quarter of the country lies below sea level.
**Het zit naast de apotheek** — for the location of a shop or office, the Dutch often use *zitten* (to sit) instead of *zijn*. *Waar zit de bakker?* sounds very native.
**Vijf minuten lopen** — distance given as travel time: *tien minuten fietsen* (ten minutes by bike). In the Netherlands, distance is almost always measured by bicycle.
**Geen dank** = you're welcome. Other options: *graag gedaan* (my pleasure), *niets te danken*, or simply *hoor*.

grammars.title: Commands
body: The simplest form in all of Dutch: **just the verb stem**, no subject, no ending.
after: For several people or formal situations, the *u* form is used: *Komt u binnen*, *Gaat u zitten* — much more polite, and common in offices and restaurants.

**Softeners are a must.** A bare command sounds rude; the Dutch slip in *even*, *eens*, or *maar*: *Kom even hier* (come here a sec), *Kijk eens* (have a look), *Ga maar zitten* (go ahead and sit down).
Prohibitions use *niet*: *Loop hier niet*, or more gently *Je mag hier niet lopen.*

grammars.title: Prepositions of place
body: Most can be guessed from their meaning, but three pairs need special attention.

head: Preposition
Meaning
Example
rows: in de stad, in het huis
op tafel, op straat, op kantoor
aan de gracht, aan de muur
tussen de bakker en de bank
bij de supermarkt, bij mijn tante

after: ⚠️ **naar** for direction, **in/op** for location: *Ik ga **naar** de stad* (I'm going to town) versus *Ik ben **in** de stad* (I'm in town).
⚠️ Some places take **op**, not *in*: *op kantoor*, *op school*, *op straat*, *op het station*, *op vakantie*. Memorize these; logic won't help.
For someone's home or business, use **bij**: *bij mijn tante*, *bij de dokter*, *bij de kapper*.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Floors are counted differently
items: *de begane grond* = the ground floor (the first floor in American usage).
*de eerste verdieping* = the Dutch first floor = the American **second** floor.
So *op de derde verdieping* means three flights up — and in a Dutch canal house, that's three steep staircases of legendary narrowness.
Elevators show **0** for the ground floor, sometimes **BG**.

blocks.text: **Het fietspad** deserves its own mention. A Dutch bike path is a real road with its own rules, and a pedestrian daydreaming on it will soon hear a far from friendly bell. It's brick red; learn the color before your first day there.

Lifesavers for when you're lost: *Ik ben verdwaald* (I'm lost), *Kunt u het op de kaart aanwijzen?* (can you show me on the map?), *Kunt u het langzaam herhalen?* (could you repeat that slowly?). The last one matters most: Dutch directions are always spoken faster than you can process in your first month.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with the right preposition.
